title: The Boundaries of the Claim
intro: The summary named the limits; this level gives the measurements behind them. What the vocabulary restriction costs in decoding accuracy, what the discarded metric actually showed and why it was discarded, how the swap rate breaks down by category, and what each theory of consciousness in the discussion was checked against.

chapters.title: The words the lens has
chapters.body:
The lens builds one direction per entry in the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]], so the concepts it can name are exactly those with a single-token name ([[single-token-limitation]]). "Prompt injection" arrives as the separate tokens prompt and injection, and a reader has to recognize that the two belong together.

The cost was measured. Across 126 multi-hop prompts whose unspoken intermediate runs from one token to four or more, the [[jacobian-lens]] places single-token intermediates in its top ten reliably and falls away sharply as the target word lengthens ([[fig-62]]). Averaging over the word's constituent tokens does not recover the loss. Swapping degrades the same way over 112 further pairs.

The [[template-lens]] closes that gap by a different route. For each of roughly 12,700 words, the authors have Claude write short passages ending just where the word would naturally fall, run the model over them, and average the residual stream at the final position; the mean is then centered against all other words and whitened ([[template-construction]]). Those vectors read and steer like lens vectors, and hold accuracy roughly constant at every word length ([[fig-61]]).

The added cost is real. The vocabulary must be enumerated in advance. A template takes a few hundred forward passes per word, against one set of backward passes per layer for the whole J-lens. And the method inherits pathologies from the [[tuned-lens]] it resembles: readouts that skip to the answer in early layers, the model's next word in the top ten only 67% of the time, and a handful of words that surface often and irrelevantly, removed by a filter the paper calls unprincipled. The [[oracle-lens]] drops the enumeration requirement at the cost of a four-stage training pipeline.

Two further limits have nothing to do with vocabulary. The readout is flat: spider, legs and eight are reported as present, with nothing about how they are bound together ([[bag-of-concepts-limitation]]). And at some positions the top tokens do not resolve into anything ([[uninterpretable-readouts]]). The paper offers three candidate causes — averaging noise, concepts without single-token names, content the authors fail to recognize — and states that it has not characterized them systematically.
chapters.childScope: Take the vocabulary limit and its two proposed repairs one at a time: the [[single-token-limitation]] and the length curve of [[fig-62]]; the construction, use and pathologies of the [[template-lens]] ([[template-construction]], [[fig-61]], [[fig-63]]); the [[oracle-lens]] pipeline ([[oracle-training]], [[reconstructor-model]], [[fig-64]]); and the two non-vocabulary limits, [[bag-of-concepts-limitation]] and [[uninterpretable-readouts]].

chapters.title: The metric it loses on
chapters.body:
The three-way comparison runs on two kinds of target ([[lens-evaluation]]). The first is a known intermediate. Six prompt distributions were assembled in which the model must compute a concept that is neither in the input nor the answer ([[intermediate-concept-benchmarks]]) — a bridging entity, a partial arithmetic result, a planned rhyme, the correct spelling of a typo. Recovery is scored with [[pass-at-k-auc]], normalized so that a method always ranking the intermediate first scores 1.

The J-lens is ahead on all six ([[fig-52]]). Its margin over the [[logit-lens]] is modest on the multi-hop and association sets and substantial on the other four. The tuned lens trails both, and on association and poetry recovers almost nothing. Those are the two sets where the next token at the readout position carries no information — a period and a newline — which is the condition under which a method biased toward next-token predictions has nothing to report.

The causal comparisons point the same way. Zeroing a lens's direction for the intermediate moves the model's output about twice as far for J-lens directions as for the other two ([[ablation-kl-effect]], [[fig-53]]), and swapping along them flips the answer more often at all three model scales ([[swap-success-rate]], [[fig-54]]).

The second target is the model's own next-token distribution, and there the J-lens is last. The tuned lens is the best match at every depth, which is what it was trained for; the J-lens carries higher divergence than even the uncorrected logit lens through most of the network ([[fig-55]]).

One measurement supports reading that loss as harmless. Below roughly a third of depth, the tuned lens's linear part is close to the identity, and stripping its learned bias collapses its readouts onto the logit lens's ([[inter-lens-agreement]]). Its predictive edge at those layers comes from the bias alone, which is to say from ignoring the input.

The choice remains a choice. No independent standard settles which job a lens should do, the six benchmarks are the paper's own construction, and every intermediate in them was picked to be a single token — the regime in which the J-lens is strongest.

chapters.title: Rates, edges and settings
chapters.body:
The broadcast result is where an average hides most. Four argument categories, four functions each, and twelve source-target pairs per function give 192 swap trials ([[function-template-protocol]]). The target-appropriate answer reaches top-1 on 76 of them, and on 101 when [[swap-strength-alpha]] is doubled ([[fig-19]]).

The per-trial grids split it by category ([[fig-68]]): country facts redirect almost perfectly, 42 of 48 off-diagonal cells reaching rank 1; months succeed partially, animals rarely, and number relations never at the default strength, 0 of 48. Failures concentrate where the source concept was barely present to begin with, measured as [[workspace-loading]]: its cosine with the residual stream in the unmodified pass. The number-word failure admits two readings the paper does not choose between: small integers may be computed outside the workspace, or their representation may not align with the number tokens' lens vectors — the vocabulary limit again.

One setting is fixed by hand. The J-space is only defined once a sparsity level is chosen, and the formalization names a value near 25 as the paper's usual choice ([[j-space-formalization]]). It agrees with an independent measurement: counted by sparse reconstruction, [[j-space-occupancy]] plateaus near 25 active vectors per position in the median case.

Both edges of the band are softer than a stated range suggests. The early boundary may be a fact about the model, if workspace content requires depth to form, or a property of the lens, since the averaged Jacobian relates each layer to the final one and the [[sensory-layers]] are far from it. The block structure marking early layers as a distinct regime does not separate the accounts. The late boundary against the [[motor-layers]] was read off lens statistics after the fact ([[workspace-boundary-metrics]]), with no principled definition separating motor from workspace; next-token predictions do sometimes appear in the middle range.

The [[open-questions]] are stated plainly. The workspace is present in the [[base-model]], so post-training did not produce it; when in pretraining it forms, and how it scales with model size, are unmeasured. Nor is there a mechanism for what puts a representation into the workspace, or a criterion predicting which computations will engage it ([[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]]).
chapters.childScope: Cover the soft numbers separately: the per-category swap grids and [[workspace-loading]] behind the 76-of-192 headline ([[fig-19]], [[fig-68]], [[function-template-protocol]]); the hand-set sparsity level against measured [[j-space-occupancy]] ([[j-space-formalization]], [[sparse-subframe]]); the two band edges and the evidence fixing them ([[sensory-layers]], [[motor-layers]], [[workspace-boundary-metrics]], [[cka]]); and the stated [[open-questions]].

chapters.title: The theories, checked one at a time
chapters.body:
The discussion restricts itself to accounts that tie consciousness to functional or computational properties ([[theories-of-consciousness]]). Against [[substrate-dependent-theories]], which make consciousness turn on physical causal structure or biological substrate, the results are declared not relevant rather than negative: they concern computation, not hardware. The paper works in the [[indicator-properties]] frame, which assesses a system on properties drawn from several theories at once, and offers the J-space as a structure those indicators can be checked against.

[[global-workspace-theory]] is handled briefly: the experiments were built around it. Limited capacity, broad composition with downstream components' input weights ([[j-space-broadcast]]), and a sharp entry rather than a gradual one ([[ignition]]) each have an analog with a number attached. The analogy is weakest at implementation: in the brain, broadcast is realized by recurrent loops and long-range cortical connections, and a forward pass has neither.

[[higher-order-theories]] locate the difference in whether a system represents its own representing. Explicit metacognitive tokens appear in the readouts, but the paper says they are not the norm. The connection it presses is structural. In [[blindsight]], visual information in a damaged field guides behavior without the patient reporting having seen anything; in the paper's automatic conditions, a line's character count drives a linebreak without entering the workspace ([[selectivity]]), and the same information enters when a question requires it. Whether the workspace version is genuinely higher-order or only more accessible is left open. Computational variants of the theory cast the higher-order state as a pointer tagging the reliability of a first-order one; the J-space instead re-encodes content in verbal form.

[[attention-schema-theory]] predicts that a system reports from a model of its own attention. Two results fit: [[experiential-reports]] are dominated by tokens naming the act of thinking and feeling, and modulation readouts surface thinking, imagine and focused at earlier layers than the content itself. The paper notes these are not models of attention as such, and sit at the edge of the theory's predictions.

[[recurrent-processing-theory]] appears to rule the architecture out. The paper's answer is that the theory's motivation is a minimum processing duration, and that serial depth, not recurrence, may be the operative property.
chapters.childScope: Give each theory its own telling against the evidence cited for it: [[global-workspace-theory]] and its three analogs ([[ignition]], [[j-space-capacity]], [[j-space-broadcast]]); [[higher-order-theories]] with [[blindsight]] and [[selectivity]]; [[attention-schema-theory]] with [[experiential-reports]], [[metacognitive-representations]] and [[thought-suppression]]; [[recurrent-processing-theory]] with the serial-depth answer; and the dismissal of [[substrate-dependent-theories]] under the [[indicator-properties]] frame.

chapters.title: Where the model and a brain part company
chapters.body:
The workspace the paper finds is built out of directions each tied to a vocabulary token ([[thinking-in-words]]). Human conscious contents are not: they mix verbal and non-verbal material. The paper gives two readings. Either the account is incomplete and the model's workspace holds more than the J-space, or [[verbalizable-representation]] really is privileged here — privileged because the model's only mode of action is emitting tokens, so a format already aligned with the vocabulary needs no translation before downstream circuits act on it. That reading carries a prediction: a model that can generate images might develop a visual component to its workspace.

A transformer also splits processing along [[two-time-dimensions]]: across layers within a position, and across the sequence through attention. The brain does not separate the two, since recurrent dynamics both refine the present interpretation and sustain the past.

The feedforward architecture is less of a difference than it appears. A feedforward stack can reproduce a recurrent network up to as many steps as it has depth ([[feedforward-emulation-of-recurrence]]). Past that, the model's only way to keep deliberating is to write intermediate results into the context and read them back ([[cot-externalization]]) — unbounded in serial depth, but interrupted at each step by the bandwidth of a token.

Attention gives the model something human cognition has no equivalent of: any representation computed earlier in the context can be retrieved, so the workspace need not hold state. Human [[working-memory]] is sharply limited and decays within seconds. [[activity-silent-working-memory]] accounts, in which items persist in transient synaptic changes and are reactivated when cued, are the nearest analog, and the paper expects models exploit it far more heavily than people do.

The workspace is fully present in a model with no Assistant and no settled point of view ([[workspace-self-dissociation]]), so the functional architecture is separable from anything playing the role of a self.

What the paper takes itself to have established is the [[llm-global-workspace-hypothesis]] as a functional and structural analogy, measured and intervened on, in one family of production models. Whether the analogy extends to [[phenomenal-consciousness]] is not tested, and no claim is made that it does.
